paragraphs: The rain fell in steady sheets as Detective Evelyn Harper stepped into the dimly lit foyer of Blackwood Manor. The news had arrived just two hours earlier: Gerald Whitaker, the wealthy businessman and owner of the estate, had been found dead in his study, a single stab wound piercing his chest. The house was eerily quiet except for the rain tapping against the window panes. Evelyn glanced around, her sharp eyes narrowing as she took in the gathered faces of the four people who had been in the house at the time of the murder. They were: Margaret Whitaker, the poised and icy wife of the deceased; Daniel Whitaker, his brash and hot-tempered son; Lila Clarke, his charming but secretive personal assistant; and Henry Caldwell, his long-time friend and house guest, who had an unsettling air of calm about him. Evelyn zipped up her raincoat and cleared her throat. “No one leaves until I find some answers.”

Evelyn began with Margaret, who stood near the grand staircase, her crimson nails tapping impatiently on the polished banister. "Gerald and I had our differences," Margaret admitted, her voice clipped, "but he was my husband. Why would I kill him when our divorce settlement was going to leave me more than comfortable?" Evelyn noted the almost rehearsed tone of her words, but it was Margaret's gaze that gave her pause; it was fixed not on her husband’s fate, but on Daniel, her stepson, with a flicker of something unreadable in her cold blue eyes. "Besides," Margaret continued, gesturing vaguely toward Henry lounging near the fireplace, "you might ask his dearest ‘friend’ over there why he was arguing with Gerald earlier tonight.” Evelyn cast a brief look at Henry, who remained silent, his calm demeanor utterly unshaken as the accusation hung heavily in the room.

Evelyn turned her attention to Henry, who lazily set down his glass of whiskey and leaned back in the antique armchair as if this were just another evening at Blackwood Manor. "Arguing with Gerald?" he said smoothly, arching a brow. "Yes, we argued. Friends do that. He'd made some... questionable investments recently, and I thought he was being reckless. But killing him? Really, Margaret, your desperation to deflect suspicion is unbecoming." His tone betrayed neither guilt nor concern, and yet Evelyn noticed his fingers trembled slightly as he adjusted his cufflinks. "Where were you when Gerald was attacked?" Evelyn asked. Henry gave a long sigh. "In the library, reading. Alone." He smirked faintly. "Not much of an alibi, I’m afraid. But then, no one else seems to have one either, Detective."

Evelyn shifted her gaze to Daniel, who had been pacing the edge of the room like a caged animal. His face was flushed, his jaw tight, and his fists clenched at his sides. "I don’t see why we’re wasting time here," he snapped, his voice bristling with anger. "It’s obvious who had the most to gain." He shot a venomous glare at Margaret, his stepmother, whose expression didn’t waver under his accusations. "She’s been after his money for years. Don’t let the grieving widow act fool you." Evelyn raised a hand to calm him. "Where were you tonight, Daniel?" For a moment, his fury faltered, and his eyes flickered toward the window. "Out on the grounds," he muttered. "I needed air after another one of Gerald's tirades. He was berating me all night, as usual." Evelyn’s sharp instincts picked up on his slip—anger laced his words, but there was also a note of guilt. His gaze darted toward Lila, the assistant, who had remained unnervingly quiet throughout the exchanges, her hands folded neatly in front of her. Evelyn filed away the interaction. Something wasn’t lining up.

Finally, Evelyn turned to Lila, who stood apart from the others, her expression meticulously composed. "And you, Miss Clarke?" Evelyn asked. "Where were you tonight?" Lila tilted her head slightly, the ghost of a smile playing at her lips. "In the kitchen, Detective. I was preparing some tea for Mr. Whitaker. He often asked for peppermint tea after his evening meetings—it helped him relax." Evelyn waited, sensing there was more. "When I brought it to his study, the door was locked," Lila added, glancing briefly at the others. "I knocked, but he didn’t respond. I thought perhaps he’d taken one of his naps in his chair. He often did that." There was a faint tremor in her voice, but it was quickly suppressed. Evelyn noticed her hands gripping the edge of her skirt tightly. "Margaret walked by the kitchen not long after," Lila added, her eyes darting toward the wife. "She seemed... tense." Evelyn raised an eyebrow at that small addition, but Lila quickly looked away, as though realizing she’d said too much.

The tension in the room thickened as Evelyn stepped toward Gerald’s study, the crime scene. She pushed open the heavy oak door, finding the once-grand room veiled in shadows. The desk was cluttered with papers, and a broken glass lay near an overturned decanter of scotch, its sharp shards glittering under the dim light. On the thick, expensive carpet, Gerald's body had already been moved by the coroner, but the dark stain of blood remained—a stark reminder of the violence. Evelyn scanned the room, noting the absence of signs of a struggle. Her eyes landed on the tea tray Lila mentioned, still sitting on the far corner of the desk. The teacup remained untouched, the liquid inside cold, its surface dark and still. A single piece of paper caught her attention—it was placed deliberately on the desk, as if meant to be found. She leaned down to read the bold, scrawled handwriting: “You’ll regret this.” There was no signature. Evelyn narrowed her eyes, her thoughts racing. The note could be a key piece of evidence—or an intentional distraction.

Evelyn exited the study and returned to the parlor, where the suspects awaited her with varying degrees of composure. She held the note aloft, letting their eyes gravitate toward it. "It seems Mr. Whitaker received a threatening message before his death. Does this mean anything to any of you?" she asked, watching them closely. Margaret’s expression didn’t change, though her fingers tightened imperceptibly on the back of a chair. Daniel scowled. "What are you implying, Detective? The man had enemies—business rivals, investors he burned. It could have come from anyone." Henry’s lips twitched into a faint, dismissive smile as he swirled the whiskey in his glass. "It sounds like Gerald to make someone regret something… but the reverse?" He shook his head slightly. Lila, who had been so controlled until now, faltered ever so slightly, her breath hitching. "I—I don't know anything about that note," she said, her voice barely audible. Evelyn caught the flicker of nervousness in her eyes, though Lila quickly looked away. Evelyn pressed her lips together, dissecting the reactions—Margaret’s steadiness unnerved her, but it was Lila’s crack in composure that stuck in her mind.

Evelyn decided to press Lila further, stepping closer and lowering her voice slightly. “You seem rattled by this note. Are you sure you’ve never seen it before?” Lila hesitated, her hands trembling before she shoved them into the pockets of her fitted blazer. “I don’t know anything about it, Detective. Gerald had plenty of enemies, as Daniel said.” But the crack in her voice betrayed her. Evelyn leaned in further. “Enemies... or someone closer to him? Someone who might have been privy to his personal affairs?” Lila’s eyes darted around the room, searching for an escape, but when she found none, she exhaled sharply. “Fine,” she said, shooting a wary look at Margaret. “There was tension lately... about work. Mr. Whitaker didn’t trust Margaret with handling certain financial accounts. He exclusively had me take care of them. And Margaret wasn’t too pleased about that.” Margaret’s icy composure cracked for the first time, her lips curling into a sneer. “You have some nerve, you little parasite,” she hissed. Evelyn didn’t miss the implicit animosity between the two women—animosity that could have boiled over. For now, she let Margaret’s retort hang, while Lila melted back into silence, shrinking slightly under the weight of what she’d revealed.

Margaret’s outburst lingered in the air, and Evelyn seized the opportunity to redirect her interrogation. "Margaret, it seems you and your husband trusted very different people. Care to explain why you didn’t approve of Lila managing the accounts?" Margaret’s sharp eyes glinted as she straightened her posture, regaining her composure. "Lila is young and... inexperienced," she replied, her voice lacquered with disdain. "Gerald had a bad habit of getting too close to his employees. I didn’t trust her motives." She cast a venomous glance at Lila, who looked away, flushed with embarrassment. Evelyn raised an eyebrow. "Too close, you say? Are you suggesting there was something more between them?" Margaret smirked faintly, though her voice softened dangerously. "I’m not 'suggesting' anything, Detective. But it wouldn’t have been the first time my husband overstepped his professional boundaries." Evelyn saw Daniel shift uncomfortably out of the corner of her eye, his fists tightening again at his sides. Whatever storm simmered beneath the surface of this family ran deep, and Evelyn began to wonder if Gerald’s supposed indiscretions had put more than one person in this room over the edge.

Evelyn turned toward Daniel, who, though trying to appear composed, looked as if he might explode at any moment. "You’re awfully quiet, Daniel," she said, her tone deliberately calm to contrast his barely contained rage. "What do you make of your stepmother’s accusations—or are you holding your tongue to protect someone?" Daniel barked a bitter laugh. "Protect someone? Don’t make me laugh, Detective. My father treated everyone like dirt—Margaret, me, his employees," he spat, shooting a pointed look at Lila. "She wasn't special. She was just another pawn he used to get what he wanted." Lila’s face burned crimson, but Daniel wasn’t finished. "He thought he could control everyone, but he couldn’t control me. And I’ll tell you right now, Detective: If you’re looking for someone who wanted him dead, you could point to any one of us. None of us had an ounce of love left for that man." His voice cracked slightly at the end, as if the admission had cost him. Evelyn tilted her head, studying his agitation. It was the fury of a man who had spent years in his father’s shadow, but the question was whether that smoldering resentment had finally boiled into murder.

As Daniel’s words hung in the air, Evelyn decided to pivot back to Henry, who had been idly watching the drama unfold with a faint smile that never quite reached his eyes. "And you, Henry," she said, her voice sharp enough to draw his full attention. "You’ve been strangely detached through all of this. Gerald trusted you—his so-called close friend—but Margaret claims you were arguing earlier. Care to elaborate?" Henry sighed, setting down his empty whiskey glass and fixing Evelyn with a cool stare. "You want the truth? Yes, Gerald and I argued," he admitted. "And it wasn’t the first time. He made a habit of turning his business woes into personal attacks, and tonight was no different." He leaned back in the chair, his calm facade never wavering. "He essentially accused me of being a leech, living off his generosity while contributing nothing." Henry shrugged, his tone almost playful. "Not entirely untrue, but I didn’t take it to heart. You don’t stay friends with someone like Gerald for decades without developing a thick skin." Evelyn studied him closely. His tone dripped with indifference, as though he were playing a part, but there was something about his nonchalance that felt... calculated. "You’re remarkably unfazed for a man whose closest friend was just murdered," she pressed. Henry smirked, his voice dropping to a purr. "Let’s just say, Detective, I’ve seen people like Gerald get what’s coming to them before. It’s rarely a surprise."

Evelyn's eyes narrowed as Henry's glib remark lingered, his words weaving an air of subtle disdain for the deceased. But before she could press him further, a hesitant cough drew her attention back to Lila. "Detective," she said, her voice soft but urgent, "I’m not saying it means anything, but... earlier tonight, while I was in the kitchen getting Gerald’s tea, I thought I heard voices from the study. Not just Gerald’s voice—there was someone else. It was... muffled, but I distinctly heard arguing." Evelyn's interest piqued as she stepped closer. "You mean you heard someone with him before you—supposedly—found the door locked?" she asked, her tone sharpening. Lila nodded quickly, glancing nervously at the others. "Yes," she insisted. "I waited a while before trying the door, but by then it’d gone quiet. I just assumed whoever it was had left." Margaret arched an eyebrow, letting out a bitter laugh. "How convenient that you ‘assumed,’ my dear. Or perhaps you’re trying to steer us away from your own involvement." Despite the jab, Evelyn caught the flicker of surprise that flashed across Margaret’s face. Was she rattled by the idea that someone else had been with her husband just before his death? Or did she already know? As Evelyn processed Lila's revelation, she couldn’t ignore the subtle shift in the room—the animosity, the tension—it felt electric now, almost ready to erupt.

Evelyn’s mind churned as she considered Lila’s claims. If someone had indeed been with Gerald before his death, the timeline of the murder could be even narrower than she thought. "Who else could have been in the study during that time?" she asked aloud, her tone more to herself than to the room. But before anyone could answer, Margaret’s voice cut through like a blade. "If there truly was someone with him," she said, her tone dripping with disdain, "then perhaps you should be looking at Daniel." All eyes turned to Gerald’s son, who stiffened visibly. "Excuse me?" Daniel shot back, his voice climbing. Margaret smirked coldly. "Oh, don’t pretend, dear. We all know you and your father were at each other’s throats constantly. Probably went in there to scream at him and things... escalated." Daniel’s face flushed crimson, and his response came in a furious bark. "You’re insane. I had nothing to do with this! You’re the one who couldn’t stand him, so don’t try to turn this around on me." Evelyn crossed her arms, watching the two of them like a hawk. Margaret’s accusation was pointed, but her delivery almost too theatrical, as if her goal was to deflect rather than pursue the truth. Daniel’s outburst only added to the friction, and Evelyn wondered if his emotions—so raw and unchecked—were a symptom of guilt or simply years of pent-up resentment.

Before the argument could spiral further, Evelyn raised a hand to silence the room, her voice cutting through with authority. “Enough. If either of you thinks accusing the other will make your own hands seem cleaner, you’re sorely mistaken.” Both Daniel and Margaret fell into a tense silence, their heated glares fixed on each other. Evelyn turned back to Lila, her mind circling the assistant’s earlier confession. “You said the voices were muffled,” she began, “but did you recognize anything distinct? A tone, a phrase, anything that might tell us who was arguing with Mr. Whitaker?” Lila hesitated, biting her lip as if weighing the consequences of her words. “I—I didn’t want to assume,” she started, her voice trembling slightly before she steadied it, “but the second voice… it sounded like Daniel’s.” The room tensed again as all eyes snapped to Daniel, who let out a furious laugh devoid of humor. “For god’s sake, this is ridiculous! Now you’re just making things up to save your own skin!” Lila shrank back but didn’t retract her statement, her eyes darting nervously to Evelyn, almost pleading. Evelyn noted the details carefully—the specific way Daniel's denial came so fast and fierce, and the flicker of real fear in Lila’s hesitation. The puzzle was growing more complex, and Evelyn knew she was edging closer to someone’s breaking point. The question was: whose?

Evelyn let the heavy silence settle before finally breaking it with deliberate calm. “Daniel,” she said evenly, “whether or not you were in the study earlier, one thing is clear—your relationship with your father was strained, to put it mildly. Tell me, how far would you go to finally get out from under his shadow?” Daniel’s eyes burned with anger as he glared at her. “You think I haven’t spent years wishing I could cut ties with that man?" he snapped, his voice trembling slightly. "But that doesn’t mean I killed him. You want to know the truth? The last time I saw him tonight was when he stormed into the study to shout at me about some bad investment he blamed me for. He said I was a disappointment—his usual rant. I left the house after that, walked down to the far end of the property to blow off steam. When I came back, he was already dead." Evelyn scrutinized him carefully, noting the defensiveness in his tone and the fleeting glance he cast toward Henry as he finished speaking. Was it a signal, an unspoken plea for solidarity—or something more? Henry, as always, remained inscrutable, just watching with that faint, unreadable smirk. Evelyn’s instincts were screaming that there was more going on between these men than what they were saying.

Evelyn’s gaze lingered on Henry, whose aloof calmness had become almost unbearable in the thickening atmosphere of accusation. Something in Daniel's quick glance toward him still nagged at her. “Henry,” she said, her voice steady but pointed, “you’ve been remarkably detached from all of this, but I noticed that Daniel keeps looking your way. Do you have something you’d like to admit about the events of tonight?” For once, Henry’s veneer cracked ever so slightly, his smirk faltering as he leaned forward in his chair, his elbows resting on his knees. “I don’t know what you’re implying, Detective,” he said, his tone slower now, more cautious. “But if Daniel’s looking at me, perhaps it’s because he knows I’ve always been a better father figure to him than Gerald ever was. Isn't that true, Danny?” Daniel flinched at the comment, his face darkening. “Don’t you dare bring me into this,” he growled, his voice low but venomous. Evelyn’s attention sharpened. Something unsaid seemed to hang between the two men, some unspoken history. Henry, sensing her curiosity, leaned back again and flashed her a smile that lacked its former confidence. “Gerald had a way of turning everyone against each other,” Henry said vaguely. “It’s no wonder we’re all suspects.” But Evelyn wasn’t convinced Henry was as unaffected by all this as he was pretending to be. For the first time, she saw cracks forming in his collected facade.

Deciding to push further, Evelyn turned back to Daniel, her curiosity piqued by his reaction to Henry’s comment. “Daniel,” she said steadily, “you seem awfully sensitive to whatever Henry just implied. What history do you two share that might be relevant here?” Daniel’s shoulders tensed, and he shot Henry a venomous glare before responding. “There’s no history,” he said quickly, his tone defensive. “Just an opportunist trying to play family friend while leeching off my father’s wealth.” Henry laughed softly, a sound that made everyone uncomfortable. “Oh, come now, Danny,” he said smoothly. “Let’s not rewrite history. You’ve always struggled with your father’s expectations, and Gerald often confided in me about his frustrations. Maybe you’re upset that I knew more about your father’s plans than you ever did.” 

Daniel’s jaw tightened, his fists clenched by his sides, and for a moment, Evelyn wondered if she were about to witness a full-blown confrontation. “Don’t twist this around, Henry,” Daniel snapped. “You may have wormed your way into his life, but you’re just as shady as anyone else in this house. He regretted trusting you—I know he did.” Evelyn caught the shift in Henry’s posture, a flicker of tension that barely registered on his polished exterior. It was subtle, but it was there. Something between these two men had clearly been simmering long before Gerald’s death, and Evelyn wondered if Gerald’s fate had been the tipping point in a long-standing rivalry. The question now was whether jealousy—or betrayal—had turned deadly.

Evelyn decided to let the animosity simmer for a moment, her eyes darting back to Lila, who seemed to be sinking further into the shadows of the room. She turned her focus to the assistant, her calm voice piercing through the mounting tension. “Lila, you’ve been quiet since you mentioned hearing the voices earlier. But if what you say is true—that Daniel was arguing with Gerald—maybe you know more than you’re letting on. After all, you were trusted enough to manage Gerald’s personal accounts. That kind of trust often leads to secrets.” Lila’s head jerked up, and for a split second, panic flashed across her face. “I’ve told you everything I know,” she said quickly, her voice higher-pitched than before. “Gerald didn’t confide in me about his problems outside of work. I didn’t even know about the note until tonight!” 

Margaret let out a sharp scoff before crossing her arms, her tone biting. “Oh, spare us the innocent act. You were practically glued to Gerald’s side half the time, always eager to listen to his complaints. You probably know more about what drove him mad than any of us.” Evelyn watched as Lila’s face crumpled momentarily, but her words were steady when she replied. “If you think I know more, it’s only because you all refused to listen to him.” She faltered then, her voice dropping almost to a whisper. “Besides, Gerald wasn’t exactly the saint you all pretend he was. He… wasn’t careful with who he upset.” 

The words sent a ripple through the room, and Evelyn honed in on the fear in Lila’s eyes as she said them. It wasn’t just fear of the others—it was fear of something, or someone, that hadn’t yet been said. Evelyn tucked the observation away carefully, though her intuition told her Lila was hiding more than just workplace anecdotes. She would have to pick that thread carefully.

Evelyn let the room fall into unease for a moment before she reached into her pocket and retrieved the ominous note from Gerald’s study. She unfolded the paper deliberately and held it up for all to see. “If this was left for Gerald tonight, as I suspect,” she said, her eyes scanning the room, “then someone here must have written it. ‘You’ll regret this.’ It’s pointed, personal, and written in haste. So I’ll ask again—who had a reason to issue such a warning?” The room was silent, all eyes darting to one another, but no one spoke. Evelyn let the weight of the words settle. 

"Margaret," Evelyn began, tilting her head slightly, "you’ve made no secret of your resentment toward your husband. Did this note come from you? A final warning to the man who controlled your life, your finances, and kept you under his thumb?” Margaret’s mouth tightened, her icy exterior momentarily cracking. “I don’t need to leave notes with my threats, Detective. If I had something to say to Gerald, I said it to his face. I’ve spent years making my peace with our arrangement.” 

Evelyn shifted her gaze to Daniel. “And you? You’ve admitted to being furious with your father tonight. Could this note represent the breaking point in your anger?” Daniel clenched his jaw so tightly that the muscles twitched, but he forced himself to speak. “I didn’t write it. Sure, I said things in the heat of the moment when we fought—plenty of things. But I didn’t kill him, and I wouldn’t leave some stupid note to scare him. That’s not my style.” 

Henry chuckled lowly from his chair. “What a charmingly brutish display, Daniel,” he said, smirking. “If you didn’t stab him, you’re certainly doing a poor job of looking innocent.” Evelyn narrowed her eyes at Henry, deciding to let his condescension slide—for now. Yet it was Lila’s expression that drew her attention. Evelyn caught it—a split-second, trembling glance at the note that she masked with downturned eyes. The assistant’s struggle to remain neutral betrayed her, and Evelyn felt certain the note tied into whatever Lila was hiding. She just had to find the right thread to pull.

Evelyn folded the note and tucked it back into her pocket, her gaze locking on Lila. “You looked at that note as if it struck a chord, Lila,” she said quietly, her voice cutting through the tension like a razor. “If there’s something you know—something you’re afraid to say—you’d better speak now. Secrets have a way of festering, and in this house, it seems everyone has something to hide.” Lila’s hands trembled as she clasped them together, her eyes darting around the room as if searching for an escape. When none appeared, she finally exhaled a shaky breath. “It’s… it’s not my note,” she stammered, her voice barely above a whisper. “But I think I might know what it’s about.”

All eyes turned to her, Margaret narrowing her gaze suspiciously, Henry’s smirk fading just slightly, and Daniel watching her like a hawk. Evelyn crossed her arms and softened her tone just enough to coax her. “Go on,” she urged. Lila swallowed hard, her pale face glistening under the tension. “Gerald found out… he found out that someone close to him was lying. About money. About trust.” She hesitated, her voice trembling as she continued. “Earlier tonight, he was furious. He told me that he couldn’t trust the people who should’ve been the closest to him. He didn’t say who, but... but I think someone was stealing from him.” 

The revelation sent a ripple through the room. Margaret’s jaw tightened, Daniel’s fists rolled at his sides, and Henry let out a low “Hmph” as if he’d suspected it all along. Evelyn kept her focus on Lila, pressing her again. “And you… if you knew this, why didn’t you tell me earlier?” Lila looked down, her voice faint. “Because I didn’t know whether it mattered. He didn’t give me names. He just said he’d put everything together—and that someone was going to pay the price for what they’d done. And now he’s dead.” Her voice broke on the final words, and Evelyn could see the regret pouring off her. But regret for what? For knowing? Or for not stopping it? The assistant was unraveling, and Evelyn knew she had to tread carefully.

Evelyn leaned in, watching the cracks in Lila’s composure deepen. "You’re telling me Gerald figured out that someone close to him—someone in this very room—betrayed him?" she pressed. Lila nodded mutely, her eyes shining with barely held-back tears. “I didn’t know what to do,” she whispered. “I told him to stay calm and handle it carefully, but Gerald… he wasn’t the kind of man who could let things go quietly.” Evelyn caught the slip in her phrasing. “Lila,” she said gently, “you knew it wasn’t just money he was unraveling, didn’t you? He'd found out something personal. You didn’t just fear for him—you feared for yourself. Didn’t you?”

Lila’s tearful eyes widened in alarm, and she instinctively took a step back. “That’s not true!” she blurted. “I wasn’t afraid for me, I swear! I…” She trailed off, her voice breaking into a sob. Before Evelyn could dig any further, Henry’s smooth voice cut in, his tone mocking. “Oh, do give the poor girl a break, Detective. You’re tormenting her, and for what? Gerald’s paranoia was hardly news to anyone here. He was always accusing someone of betrayal. Tonight was no different.” Henry’s nonchalance seemed calculated, but Evelyn caught the subtle tension in his otherwise casual posture. He was watching her, watching them all, as though trying to maintain a control he wasn’t as confident in as he wanted to appear.

Daniel, however, wasn’t so composed. “If something shady was going on with my father’s accounts,” he said icily, “then maybe you should be looking at Henry. He’s the one who’s been milking his so-called friendship with my dad for years. God knows how much money he’s wasted on you!” 

Henry raised an eyebrow, his smirk flashing back like a shield. “Really, Daniel? That’s the best you’ve got? You should tread carefully—your father’s ‘disappointment’ in you might not just have been personal. Bank statements don’t lie.” The tension escalated, bubbling to the surface, and Evelyn absorbed it all, her instincts tightening around the invisible threads binding this group’s lies together. There was something here—something about Gerald’s discovery tonight and the betrayal he felt that tied directly to his death.

Evelyn’s patience had thinned. She stepped forward, her voice rising above the squabbling. “Enough! I’m not interested in your snide comments or your attempts to point fingers at one another. Someone in this room knew exactly what Gerald had uncovered tonight. Someone was desperate enough to silence him before he could act.” She turned sharply to Henry. “You seem very sure of yourself, Henry. For a man who claims to have been in the library all night, you certainly know a lot about what happened in Gerald’s mind before his death. How did you know about his distrust? About his accounts?”

Henry’s smirk twitched, barely holding. “It wasn’t a secret,” he replied coolly. “I told you before—Gerald was paranoid. He talked to me about his suspicions plenty of times. If he thought someone was betraying him, he wouldn’t have kept quiet about it. Not to me, at least.”

Evelyn folded her arms, her gaze unrelenting. “And yet, for all your so-called friendship, you argued with him tonight. You admitted it yourself. Perhaps he found out something about you—something you were doing behind his back.” 

Henry’s posture stiffened, but he forced a chuckle. “You’re barking up the wrong tree, Detective. If Gerald had truly found something damning on me, we wouldn’t have stopped at a quarrel. He loved theatrics—you know that—you’ve seen it tonight, haven’t you? No, if Gerald found out who was betraying him, he’d have confronted them directly.” 

His words hung in the air like bait, but Evelyn didn’t bite, not yet. Instead, she turned to Margaret. “What about you? Did Gerald confront you tonight with proof of his suspicions?” Margaret’s lips curled into a thin, practiced smile. “I’m sure I don’t know what you’re implying,” she said icily. “If Gerald suspected me of anything, it’s because he couldn’t face the consequences of his own short-sighted decisions. Whatever betrayal he thought he uncovered had nothing to do with me.”

But Evelyn wasn’t convinced. The cracks were spreading, layer by layer, and she could feel she was getting closer to unveiling the truth—however tangled it might be.

Evelyn’s gaze darted back to Lila, who was shaking like a leaf, her earlier composure completely shattered. “Lila,” she said firmly, taking a step toward her. “I don’t think you’re telling me everything. You were the closest to Gerald tonight, the last person to see him alive apart from the killer. He trusted you with his finances, his personal affairs—if he discovered a betrayal, then you’d know more about it than anyone. What aren’t you saying?”

“No! I didn’t—I didn’t do anything!” Lila cried, tears streaming down her face now. “Yes, he trusted me, and yes, he was angry when I saw him tonight, but it wasn’t because of me!” She stammered, her breathing ragged, before blurting out, “It was Margaret! Gerald finally figured out what she’d been doing—taking money from the accounts, siphoning it into private accounts abroad. He wanted to confront her that night, Detective, and he was furious.” 

Every head in the room whipped toward Margaret, who stood rooted in place, her face a mask of shock that quickly hardened into fury. “That’s absurd!” she hissed, venom dripping from her voice. “This little sycophant has always been desperate for attention. If anything, I’d accuse her of trying to cover her own tracks. Perhaps you were the one forging documents, Lila, and you knew your time was running out.”

But Evelyn caught it—the way Margaret’s hands tightened into fists, her body tensing as though she were ready to pounce. Lila’s accusation might have been tinged with desperation, but Margaret’s reaction wasn’t merely defensive—it spoke of someone who had just been cornered. Evelyn let the words settle into the thick air of the room, but her instincts screamed that Margaret wasn’t working alone. This wasn’t just about dirty money—someone else was tangled in the web of lies and anger Gerald had stumbled into before his death.

Before Evelyn could respond, Daniel’s voice roared through the room, his face twisted with anger. “Of course it was Margaret!” he yelled, his voice shaking. “She’s been trying to bleed him dry for years! She never cared about him—she didn’t even try to hide it. And when he finally caught on, she panicked and—” 

“Shut your mouth, Daniel!” Margaret snapped, her control slipping, her face livid. “If anyone had a reason to kill Gerald, it was you! You hated your father and made no secret of your temper. Don’t think I didn’t hear you shouting outside his study earlier. God knows what you’d have done in a rage!”

Daniel opened his mouth to retort, but Evelyn stepped between them, her voice sharp as steel. “Quiet!" she demanded, and the room fell starkly silent. She turned to Daniel, her voice lowering but losing none of its impact. “You were outside the study, then?” 

Daniel froze, realizing too late that Margaret had exposed him. His shoulders sagged slightly, the fight draining from him. “Yeah,” he muttered finally, his voice hoarse. “After our argument, I went back to yell at him. But when I got there, I heard voices. I thought he was meeting with someone, so I left.” 

Evelyn’s eyes were like knives. “Who was the other voice? Did you recognize it?” 

Daniel shook his head quickly. “It was low, but… no, I couldn’t tell. And I didn’t stay to listen. I swear to you, Detective—I didn’t kill him. When I came back later, the house was quiet. I didn’t even know he was dead until the screaming started.” 

But Evelyn saw something flicker across his face—fear, guilt? It wasn’t clear. Margaret let out a cold, mirthless laugh. “How convenient,” she said. “Poor Danny just happened to walk away at the perfect moment.” 

But Evelyn wasn’t looking at Daniel anymore. Her eyes had shifted to Henry, who had remained startlingly quiet during the exchange. His smirk was gone, and for the first time, unease flickered over his polished demeanor. A bead of sweat traced down his temple, and Evelyn’s gut tightened. She had him. She was certain of it. “Henry,” she said, her voice soft but deadly as she spun to face him. “I think it’s time we had a little heart-to-heart, don’t you?”

Henry’s calm facade finally shattered as Evelyn stepped toward him, her voice cutting through the mounting tension like a blade. “You’ve been playing a very careful game tonight, Henry,” she said, her eyes locked on his. “Too careful. All your smooth deflections and smug remarks were meant to keep attention off you, but the truth has a way of slipping through the cracks.”

Henry exhaled sharply, his polished exterior crumbling as his shoulders sagged. “This is absurd,” he muttered, though his voice had lost its edge. “Why would I kill Gerald? I stood to gain nothing from his death.”

“Oh, but you did,” Evelyn countered quickly. “You said it yourself—Gerald accused you of being a leech, a wasted investment. It wasn’t just an argument. He realized you’d been taking advantage of him all these years, skimming money from his investments, and he was finally ready to cut you out of his life—and his will. That’s what he told you tonight, didn’t he? That he knew the truth and you were done. You weren’t ready to lose your easy life, were you, Henry?”

The silence that followed was deafening, save for the rain still hammering against the windows. Henry’s hands shook, but his face twisted into something between desperation and arrogance. “You’re bluffing,” he said hoarsely. “You have no proof.”

Evelyn smirked ever so slightly, pulling out the ominous note once more. “This was your last-ditch effort to scare him into silence, wasn’t it? But Gerald was never one to be intimidated. So when the argument escalated, you panicked, didn’t you? You stabbed him, Henry. Not because you planned it, but because you couldn’t face the consequences of being exposed.” She leaned in closer, her voice dropping to a whisper. “And the real kicker? You didn’t realize he’d locked the study door after you. That’s why Lila found it locked when she came with the tea, isn’t it?”

Henry’s composure finally crumbled completely, his face pale and slick with sweat. He opened his mouth to deny it, but the strength had left him. Instead, he slumped back into his chair, defeated. “He… he pushed me too far,” Henry murmured, his voice cracking. “He couldn’t see it—everything I did for him, for this… this damn house. He always looked at me like I was nothing.”

Evelyn straightened, her gaze hard. “Enough,” she said coldly. “It’s over.” The room was silent, the tension deflating all at once, leaving only the echoes of Henry’s confession hanging in the air. As the police arrived to take him away, Evelyn glanced at the others. Margaret, Daniel, and Lila all seemed stunned, shaken by how close they had each danced to the edge of suspicion. But Evelyn, as always, had unraveled the truth, no matter how tangled it had been. The rain began to lighten outside, and with it, the oppressive weight over Blackwood Manor eased. Another case closed—but the scars left in its wake would linger for far longer.
